items.title: She Tried to Live as a Man Before Detransitioning. Now, Her Story Is Part of a Powerful Book and Podcast Series
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Author Paul Hastings is on a mission to share powerful stories about “ordinary people” inspired by an “extraordinary God.”

In fact, that’s part of the title of his book, “Compelled: Ordinary People Extraordinary God,” a project that shares incredible testimonies of people who have gone from darkness to light, have faced difficult circumstances — and found freedom.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Hastings, who hosts a podcast by the same name, said his mission to tell such powerful stories developed after years of working full-time in politics.

“I got really burned out, as you could imagine, just like the political cycle always, always on,” he said. “And so my wife and I just began praying like, ‘Lord, there are other things that you know I could do.’ And one thing that I was convicted about is that the whole time that I was in the political sphere, I had never once stopped to pray for my political opponents. I just cared about their personal destruction, which just sounds terrible, but I’m just being honest.”

This conviction led Hastings deeper into prayer, and he reflected on how God can change any heart, regardless of how terrible a person has behaved. This became the root of the “Compelled” podcast. The book simply builds upon that effort.

“The whole premise of the podcast, the radio show, and the book ‘Compelled’ is to find people with these amazing stories that their life truly exemplifies what it means to live a life compelled by Christ,” Hastings said. “So stories of stark transformation.”

He had to narrow over 100 stories down to just seven for the book, including everything from people who have been missionaries to cannibal tribes in Papua New Guinea to a mom who was falsely accused of murder and sentenced to life in prison.

“Each of these people has an amazing testimony … Christ just radically transformed who they are and how they lived,” Hastings said. “And trying to choose the top seven to place into our book was not an easy feat. That was probably one of the hardest tasks about the book, but hopefully we did a good job.”

Hastings said one of the stories that most stuck with him was Laura Perry Smalts, a woman who previously identified as transgender and lived for years as a man before finding Christ.

“When she was in her early 20s, she made a decision to reject everything that she’d ever been taught,” he said. “She thought that she would find answers by transgendering herself into a man. And so over the course of 10 years, she surgically removed every female organ from her body.”

Ultimately, after altering her body, going on testosterone, and growing a beard while living as an individual named “Jake,” Smalts changed her heart and mind.

“Today, Laura lives a completely different life than the one that she once lived,” he said, noting she has shared her testimony. “And it’s just an incredible testimony of the Lord’s goodness and kindness that no one is too far gone, that the Lord can save anybody in any type of circumstance.”

Ultimately, Hastings said he wants people to know it’s never too late to change.

“The Lord can save anybody,” he said. “So if you’ve got an aunt, an uncle, a child, and a cousin, a friend, a neighbor, and you think to yourself, ‘Man, this person is too far gone. They’re too far lost. They cannot be redeemed.’ That’s not true. … The Lord can take the most hardened sinner and transform their life.”

items.title: Do Prophets Still Exist? Meet the Filmmaker Who’s Investigating This Biblical Phenomenon
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Interesting.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Matthew Thayer is on a mission to explore whether modern-day prophets are still delivering important messages.

Thayer’s new film, “Can You Hear Me Now?” tackles this timeless topic, exploring whether the biblical dynamic of prophets delivering God’s Word to humanity is still alive and active today.

The film director said he “absolutely” believes God still speaks through prophets, explaining his perspective that individuals with this ability happened to “just kind of show up in the Bible.”

“There’s nothing that actually says, ‘Oh, this is what a prophet is,’ and so what that means to me is that the ancient Middle East — they were just there,” Thayer said of biblical prophets. “So the people of that era and the people that were originally receiving the words of the Bible originally just understood what a prophet was and a prophet’s function.”

The director believes it’s been proven that people have had dreams and experiences they can’t explain — sequences that tell them what will happen; Thayer said these are often quite accurate. He believes that’s because God has enabled them, through Him, to witness elements of the unseen realm.

When asked why some people in the church world might dismiss modern-day prophecy, Thayer held little back.

“Honestly, I think it’s because the dark spiritual forces that we war against, according to Ephesians 6, knew that communications with God was the first thing that they needed to take out,” he said. “Communications are taken out in warfare first … that’s just a standard warfare practice, and, so, if we are actually in a spiritual war, it would make sense that they would target prophets first.”

Thayer advocated being careful about the sources people gather their prophecy from, as false prophets can open people up to deception. Thus, discernment is key.

“To me, it’s more about who the prophet is pointing to,” he said. “Because that’s what Deuteronomy 13 very clearly stipulates … that there’s going to be false prophets and they’re going to be accurate. But if they’re pointing you away from Yahweh, if they’re pointing you away from God, then they’re a false prophet.”

Thayer understands some of the hesitation people have surrounding prophecy, explaining that his own skepticism came when politics and prophecy collided. He said it felt like some of those making proclamations — especially surrounding President Donald Trump in 2016 — felt like they didn’t quite land. But, over time, the volume of so-called “words” surrounding Trump shocked him.

“The amount of words that were coming out just kind of made me go, like, ‘I think God’s actually trying to do something,'” he said. “He’s trying to alert people to what’s going on and so that’s kind of one of the things that I was exploring with the documentary.”

Thayer recalled being in an auditorium in 2007, when faith leader Kim Clement offered up a prophecy many saw as predicting Trump’s presidency.

“We’re all standing there going like, ‘What? Like the apprentice guy? What?'” Thayer recalled, noting how Clement said Trump would be a trumpet. “Well, what does a trumpet do? A trumpet calls to attention, a trumpet calls people to action, and that’s actually really kind of very close to what [Trump’s] doing — like he’s pointing at things that we didn’t even know existed, and darkness, and corruption that was happening within our government.”

items.title: Beijing Police Detained a Pastor and Seven Church Members as They Set Up for Their 20th Anniversary Service
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: A Beijing pastor and seven members of his church have been held in criminal detention for nearly a month after police broke up preparations for the underground church’s 20th anniversary celebration, according to a letter from the pastor’s wife published this week by the religious-freedom group China
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

A Beijing pastor and seven members of his church have been held in criminal detention for nearly a month after police broke up preparations for the underground church’s 20th anniversary celebration, according to a letter from the pastor’s wife published this week by the religious-freedom group ChinaAid.

On the evening of Sept. 4, about 50 members of Beijing Jiaquan Church were setting up a hotel conference room for the next day’s celebration when more than 100 officers, some in plainclothes, surrounded the room, the letter says. Everyone was made to hand over their state ID numbers, addresses and phone numbers before being sent home.

Pastor Zhou Zixun and seven church members were held on suspicion of fraud. Two were later released and two more leaders were picked up, so as of this week eight people are still in criminal detention. Their families don’t know where they’re being held, and some were taken without medication for chronic conditions, the letter says.

According to Cui, the fraud accusation is tied to Jiaquan’s status as an unregistered house church and its ministry finances. Jiaquan, founded in 2006, has more than 1,000 members across several cities and runs a music school that trains worship leaders for other house churches. China permits Protestant worship through state-sanctioned organizations, while independent house churches operate outside that system and face government restrictions.

“Despite China’s own constitution warranting religious freedoms, the government will not allow a church to register unless they give authorities full control,” wrote Cui Jinyoung, Zhou’s wife and the church’s co-founder, who is South Korean and has been barred from re-entering China for about three years. “Therefore most churches throughout China remain unregistered and are considered illegal. Jia Quan Church is no exception and this is the basis for their fraud accusations.”

The account comes from Cui and ChinaAid, a U.S.-based Christian human-rights organization. ChinaAid said when it first reported the detentions that it was still working to independently confirm details. The broader crackdown on independent churches, however, is well documented. Last October, police arrested nearly 30 pastors and members of Zion Church across seven cities and charged its founder, Ezra Jin Mingri, with “illegal use of information networks.”

Jin was released in July after President Trump raised his case with Xi Jinping, but eight Zion members are still being held on fraud and “illegal business” charges, with a trial that keeps getting pushed. Early Rain Covenant Church in Chengdu, whose pastor has been in prison since 2019, had more than 30 people detained in a June raid and 11 more, most of them over 60, picked up at a teahouse Bible study three weeks ago.

And since Jan. 1, a revised public-security law has for the first time named “illegal religious activities” as an offense police can punish on the spot with up to 15 days’ detention.

“We are especially concerned by the use of the criminal charge of ‘fraud,’” ChinaAid founder Bob Fu said in a statement Tuesday. “We have seen similar economic-crime accusations increasingly used against house church pastors and coworkers in connection with ordinary religious ministry, church offerings and other church activities.”

Pew’s most recent comparable survey estimate found roughly 20 million Chinese adults formally identified as Christian in 2018, about 90 percent of them Protestant. Pew also cautions that religious identity is unusually difficult to measure in China and that estimates vary widely, in part because many Christians worship in unauthorized house churches.

Cui’s letter closes with a request for prayer for her husband and, she writes, for “the pastors and co-workers of churches across China who are suffering similar persecution.”

items.title: ‘Resident Evil’: The Evil and Fear That Resides in Every Man
items.author: Dr. Kody W. Cooper
items.summary:
Dr. Kody W. Cooper

In a culture where big government allied with big pharma push autonomous individualism via abortion drugs, the man of virtue who resists appears to be a monstrosity.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Kody W. Cooper

Personally, I was not a “Playstation kid,” but all 90s-era kid video gamers knew about Resident Evil. In an American suburb, Raccoon City, a shadowy pharmaceutical corporation has been experimenting with viruses to create biological weapons, including human mutants. Predictably, there is an outbreak transforming huge swaths of the populace into zombies. It was a groundbreaking survival-horror game in which the player explores eerie mansions and zombie-infested streets, relying on his sidearm and wits. The game spawned one of the most successful and influential video-game franchises of all time. And the films based on it were early examples of successful Hollywood adaptations of video games. 

The reboot film that recently came out, Resident Evil (rated R for pervasive language and violence), is a noteworthy entry into the franchise not only because it is a well-made thriller/horror film that introduces the franchise to a new generation but also because of its deeply pro-fatherhood and pro-life message hidden under layers of metaphor. Warning: spoilers follow.

The film is set in Racoon City the same night as the events of the Resident Evil 2 game when the Umbrella Corporation’s bioweapon virus caused a zombie outbreak. But it is reimagined with contemporary technology, like smartphones, and follows a new character, Bryan (played ably by Austin Abrams). The film opens with Bryan taking a mystery medical package to be delivered to Raccoon City, driving through a blizzard. He takes a phone call from his girlfriend Michelle, who wants to continue their discussion of the recent revelation that she is pregnant. Bryan is clearly afraid of becoming a father and exhorts her to take another test. He then expresses indifference about whether Michelle should get an abortion: “It’s your body, your choice,” he lamely says, to which she takes offense. She pleads with him to come home so they can discuss it as he protests that he has an important job to deliver the mystery medical package. “This is the life that I’m carrying, right now,” he says, before getting cut off and running over a woman who jumps out into the middle of the road.

As director Zach Cregger puts it, the movie is only on the surface a zombie apocalypse. What it’s really about is the fear of prospective parents having children in a world that “just seems to be getting worse and worse?”

Thus Bryan’s night of horrors begins. He finds the woman alive, acting strangely but apparently not entirely zombified and brings her to the car, buckles her in, and starts speeding her to the hospital before getting pulled over by a police officer. The officer agrees to help transport her, but they make it only a mile down the road before the police car crashes. He investigates to find the officer dead, and then the woman—now fully zombified—chases him around the car as he shouts, “Leave me alone!” And he shoots her.

There has been speculation online about what it all might mean. While the following is just my interpretation, I believe that the metaphor is apparent. The woman is a metaphor for Bryan’s girlfriend, Michelle. The allusion of the scene is to that all-too-familiar episode young fathers face: speeding one’s “knocked up” wife to the hospital to deliver the baby. But faced with the scariness of a pregnant girlfriend, who is undergoing the bodily and psychological changes wrought by another “parasitical” being inside of her, Bryan runs. 

He arrives at a farmhouse seeking refuge with a picture of an apparently happy older couple. In other words: the man running from his responsibility returns to his parents. But, the virus has spread there too. The elderly zombie woman screams at Bryan and attacks him. Like a good mother, she scolds Bryan for running from the responsibilities of fatherhood. Or is she (also?) Bryan’s mother-in-law? Either way, Bryan shoots his metaphorical zombie-Mom and then sees zombie-Michelle sprinting across the lawn. No matter where he goes, those to whom he is bound will follow. He shoots zombie-Michelle but watches in horror as tendrils stretch out of her to join with and fuse to zombie-Mom, forming a hideous one-flesh, many-limbed, tumbleweed-like monster that cartwheels after him. 

Now running from his “parents” and his “girlfriend,” Bryan happens upon a young girl, maybe eight years old, hiding in an RV bathroom. She reports that her mother bit her foot and ran off. The foot is mutating, but she seems fine otherwise. Bryan is filled with compassion and agrees to help her, before she too mutates and attacks him. She bites him, and he ultimately shoots her too. “That wasn’t real. That didn’t happen,” he tells himself, “I didn’t shoot a little girl; I love children.”

Bryan sees the need of young girls for a father, whose office it is to protect them from monsters. Bryan grasps this and tries to help this metaphor for his unborn daughter. But embracing fatherhood will mean embracing a metamorphosis, which her bite begins. It is a metamorphosis men experience when their wives show them that first positive pregnancy test.

Bryan runs again. He now encounters the Umbrella Corporation agents, who reveal to him that the package he is carrying is the antidote to the virus spreading, which they must deliver to the pharmaceutical lab in the city center. Bryan’s newfound companions fire a machine gun to drive off the tumbleweed monster, which has apparently engulfed others, including the little girl. 

It has become apparent the tumbleweed is a metaphor for the change Bryan must embrace by accepting the responsibilities of manhood. It represents all the relationships that must transform a boy into a man: being a responsible husband, father, son, son-in-law, and friend. Running from these responsibilities for refuge in friendship does not work either. For Bryan’s new companions quickly die, and they get engulfed into the tumbleweed. The idea is that friends are transformed by your choices, and true friends would encourage you to embrace the change and responsibility. And, finally, true friends will strengthen you and help bear the load of marriage and parenthood.

Now, Bryan takes up the mantle of finishing the job. He runs through sewers and streets toward the Umbrella Corp. and must ascend from the basement garage to the laboratory on the top floor. The man running from manhood seeks meaning in his work—but this is not satisfying either. In a touching moment, he gazes upon a stick figure family bumper decal. He pulls out his phone to record a message for Michelle. He admits to being afraid of responsibility and parenthood but says he does want to have a kid with her, and he tells her she would be an amazing mom. 

Then he ascends, and the tumbleweed monster returns. A vomiting zombie spewing melting acid attacks, and he grabs it, forcing it to spew at the tumbleweed. This fails to appease it. Mere words aren’t enough—he has to embrace fatherhood with his entire being. The bite from the little girl is spreading the infection, and his bodily transformation has begun. 

One last obstacle remains: a maternity ward full of newborn children. It is a disturbing and gruesome scene because the zombie virus has spread its tentacles here too, transforming the newborns into monsters. Bryan runs from the zombie babies. And, having complained the whole movie about his inabilities to use a real gun—they are much harder to handle in real life than in video games—he successfully uses his last bullet to shoot a small target to open a door and unleash the zombie children to knock down the tumbleweed and escape again. He shouts: “Video games!” It is a powerful metaphor for the feckless, basement-dwelling male of the twenty-first century, whose final refuge to avoid the responsibilities of manhood is video gaming.

In the climactic scene, he delivers the “cure,” which they use to synthesize a vial of green medicine. His metamorphosis now speeds up, and the not-quite-zombified monster-Bryan desperately attacks the scientists. “Help me!” he implores as the tumbleweed finally catches up and fuses itself with him. Having spoken the words to agree to embrace manhood, the change comes fast and furious, and old cowardly Bryan cries out one last time. He is desperate to undo what has been done, to use the shady pharmaceutical company’s drug to kill the virus that now reveals itself to be a metaphor for his unborn child all along, the unleashing of which was brought on by him running over (“knocking up”) his girlfriend. He is the source of the scary, life-altering, and metamorphizing force that is new human life. The “antidote”—the life he was “carrying right now”, his own—promises to preserve his autonomous self by killing the tumbleweed, i.e., killing his relationship with Michelle, the child, his friends, and all the transformative relationships marriage and children bring into the world.

In the last moment, he desperately tries to induce the chemical abortion, but fails. As the governmental helicopters arrive, a massive monster-Bryan, now transformed, roars in defiance of both big government and big pharma.

The man who embraces husbandhood and fatherhood must become a kind of monster, powerful enough to protect those he is charged to care for. And in a culture that celebrates the power of big government allied with big pharma to push autonomous individualism via abortion drugs, the man of virtue who resists appears to be a monstrosity. Only on the surface does the “resident evil” win. The evil that resides in the heart of every man is the fear of losing his lusty autonomy, the fear of responsibility. This is the pro-choice evil that Bryan finally conquers.

items.title: Flannery O’Connor and the Spiritual Quest of Gen Z
items.author: Fr. Damian Ference
items.summary:
Fr. Damian Ference

Just as the COVID-19 pandemic was a significant formative experience for Gen Z, so too was it for Flannery O’Connor, or at least her legacy.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Fr. Damian Ference

The College Beat: ARTICLE XVIII

. . .

In the past few months, The New York Times, The Atlantic, and the Wall Street Journal have all published stories on the renewed interest of Generation Z in faith and religion. Gen Z, born between 1997 and 2012, never experienced life without the internet, do not remember air travel before the events of 9/11, and suffered the unprecedented lockdowns and social restrictions of a global pandemic during their most formative years. Yet, many young men and women of this generation, currently in their teens and twenties, are unapologetically seeking to quench their spiritual thirsts in traditional religion. In this essay I hope to show how Flannery O’Connor—who kept a prayer journal documenting her own spiritual journey during her early twenties—would not be surprised by the spiritual quest of Gen Z, or that many of them are finding their place in her beloved Catholic Church. 

I will begin by demonstrating how the experience of the COVID-19 pandemic acted as a moment of grace for Generation Z, offering transformation of mind and heart to things beyond this world. Second, I will show how Flannery O’Connor stands as a strange yet credible witness to an authentic way of life that offers meaning and truth to members of a generation longing to be part of something bigger than themselves. Third, I will argue that reading the stories, letters, essays, and prayers of Flannery O’Connor allow Generation Z an opportunity to reflect on their own lives and interpret their experiences in a context that both challenges and comforts their habit of being.

The COVID-19 Pandemic as Grace 

To consider the COVID-19 pandemic and all the lockdowns and restrictions that followed from it “a grace” may seem ridiculous to many, but not to Flannery O’Connor, or to those who give papers about her at academic conferences. For in a letter to John Hawkes dated April 14, 1960, O’Connor explains, “Grace, to the Catholic way of thinking, can and does use as its medium the imperfect, purely human, and even hypocritical.” It is the grace that arrives after your family is murdered in the woods and you are face-to-face with the Misfit, or when your leg is stolen in a barn by a traveling Bible salesman, or when you crash a tractor into a tree, setting is ablaze and losing your shoes, or when you accidentally shoot your mother instead of the slut, or when you are assaulted by a fat girl of eighteen or nineteen with bad acne in the waiting room of a doctor’s office. These are all terrible things—terrible experiences, but they are also all moments of grace in the fiction of Flannery O’Connor, moments in which her characters are afforded an opportunity for repentance, healing, and redemption—a new way of seeing, a new way of living, a new way of being. O’Connor writes, “There is a moment in every great story in which the presence of grace can be felt as it waits to be accepted or rejected, even though the reader may not recognize this moment.” 

Very few people were calling the pandemic a grace when we were going through it six years ago. I was a doctoral student in Rome at the time, already under government lockdown, writing a dissertation on Flannery O’Connor when the American embassy called our rector and told him that we all had to go home. After packing a suitcase full of books and shaving my beard down to a mustache so that the mask would seal over my face, I flew out of Fiumicino airport on March 24, 2020, and landed in Cleveland a little after midnight the next day, Flannery O’Connor’s birthday. Because I had arrived from Italy, which was the epicenter of the pandemic, I had to quarantine for two weeks and take my temperature twice a day and report it to the county healthy board when they called me at three o’clock in the afternoon each day. Fortunately for me, as a Gen X celibate doctoral student who was used to long periods of solitude, I kept to the writing schedule I had in Rome, and it kept me sane. But it was an entirely different story for Gen Z. 

During the spring of 2020 across the US schools and churches and many businesses closed their doors, while social distancing, constant handwashing, masking, and online classes became the norm. For the older members of Gen Z, Spring sports, musical performances, and theatre productions were cancelled, along with prom, and in some cases, even graduation ceremonies. Weddings, if they happened at all, became restricted and intimate events with only a few family members and friends. If your loved ones were in a hospital or a nursing home, visits became tricky, if they happened at all, and not without PPE (personal protective equipment). The world went from in-person to online, and a generation that already spent an inordinate amount of time attached to screens was exacerbated by pandemic protocols. Moreover, Gen Z had already reported higher rates of anxiety and depression than previous generations, but the numbers climbed “steeply upward after 2020.” More depression, more anxiety, more suicidal ideation. 

Where is the grace? How could all this apparent “bad news” about Gen Z’s pandemic experience bring about anything good? Perhaps at this point we ought to turn to O’Connor herself, specifically a line from the first entry of her prayer journal. “Please help me get under things and find where you are,” O’Connor writes. Even if we don’t believe in God or choose not to pray like O’Connor did, we ought to notice that many members of Generation Z did want help to “get under things” and to find God after their pandemic experience, as many of them reported wanting to be part of something that was “bigger than themselves.” In a recent interview with Vox, one member of Gen Z put it this way: “I did not grow up going to church. My family never went to church when I was younger, but I always had questions and felt like something bigger was out there. . . . So as soon as I could drive myself, I went to church and started looking for those answers.” 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

A 2025 Pew Research poll reported that “recent polling shows no clear evidence of a religious revival among young adults,” although the same report noted that the decline of Christianity has stabilized and that “there are some interesting things happening with religion among young people.” One of those interesting things is that Gen Z is finding a home in O’Connor’s Roman Catholic Church, as the average American diocese saw about 38 percent more people joining the Church in 2026 compared with 2025. The New York Times interviewed Archbishop Mitchell Thomas Rozanski of St. Louis about the recent surge of young converts and he said, “I think technology has isolated us from one another. I think that COVID just really magnified the situation. We are realizing that many of the ills of our society, particularly anxiety and depression, come about from that isolation.” 

Gen Z can be likened to Hazel Motes in Flannery O’Connor’s first novel Wise Blood. It is only when Haze loses everything—in the scene where patrolman pushes Haze’s car over the embankment – that he begins his turn back to God. That is grace at work. And I argue it is that same saving grace that was at work on Generation Z during the pandemic, whether anyone noticed it or not. And it is that same grace which is now being accepted, certainly not by every member of Generation Z, but by enough of them to make The New York Times take interest.  

Flannery O’Connor as an Authentic Human Witness

In her 2023 book, Generations, Jean Twenge reports that Gen Z is “concerned with authenticity.” At first glance this desire for authenticity may not seem novel, for young people of every generation have been marked with a desire for what is real and true, but a closer look reveals that there is a notable gravitas on display in Gen Z’s relationship to authenticity, particularly because of the ubiquity and perceived threat of AI. In recent weeks, across the country at college graduation ceremonies, “listeners have balked as commencement speakers have either told them to embrace artificial intelligence, or have otherwise mentioned the ever-expanding technology in a speech.” Gen Z graduating classes have literally booed such speakers. They want authentic human encounters, and they value authentic humans. 

The Gen Z actor and musician, Maya Hawke, found that authentic human witness in Flannery O’Connor. She explains, “I was assigned Flannery O’Connor by my English teacher, and I wanted to do some extra reading. I found her prayer journal. And then I read it and loved it. And I knew that my dad had always been extremely interested in smart people who are interested in God. It’s a very large class of people that exist, and they’re kind of underrepresented. And the prayer journal is this smart young woman who was really, really interested in her faith and God.” 

Although Pew Research Center has not yet polled Gen Z on how Flannery O’Connor has impacted their world view, anecdotally, as one who has taught O’Connor to Gen Z and as one who spends of lot of his time ministering to Zoomers, I want to make a case for Flannery O’Connor as a model of authentic human witness. 

Louise Abbot, one of O’Connor’s closest friends described Flannery in this way: “I never saw any kind of contradiction or inconsistency. It seemed to me that another gift she has was that she was always sincere. . . . Even in the company of other people, she was always herself.” Robert Giroux, O’Connor’s editor and dear friend said, “We knew she was as honest as the day is long, and that was just part of her nature. At least I felt I knew it, upon meeting her, just talking to her. And you can do it with most people. I mean, you can really tell almost immediately.” St. Thomas Aquinas, one of O’Connor’s intellectual heroes, taught that human beings are agents of truth, that we are made to know truth and we take delight in knowing it. When truth is embodied in a human person, we call it integrity or authenticity, and that is what we find in the person of Flannery O’Connor. 

What makes Flannery O’Connor a most attractive artist and such an esteemed human being to so many of us—and, I argue, increasingly, members of Generation Z—is her near perfect balance of confidence and humility. On one hand she acknowledges her giftedness as a writer: “I write because I write well,” while on the other hand she does not neglect the Giver of that gift: “Don’t let me ever think, dear God, that I was anything but the instrument for Your story—just like the typewriter was mine.” 
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

Flannery O’Connor was one of the greatest Catholic artists of the twentieth century and was a masterful Christian apologist, insisting, “I am no disbeliever in spiritual purpose and no vague believer. I see from the standpoint of Christian orthodoxy. This means that for me the meaning of life is centered in our redemption by Christ and what I see in the world I see in its relation to that.” Yet, this confidence in Christian orthodoxy does not position her above others. She writes to Louise Abbot, “I don’t set myself up to give spiritual advice but all I would like you to know is that I sympathize and I suffer this way myself. When we get our spiritual house in order, we’ll be dead. This goes on. You arrive at enough certainty to be able to make your way, it is making it in darkness. Don’t expect faith to clear things up for you. It is trust, not certainty.”

As a Catholic, O’Connor embraced a high standard for sexual morality, although she witnessed its opposite during her time at Yaddo: “In such a place you have to expect them all to sleep around. This is not sin but Experience, and if you do not sleep with the opposite sex, it is assumed that you sleep with your own.” However, O’Connor also notes that, “Purity strikes me as the most mysterious of the virtues and the more I think about it the less I know about it,” and that, “Anyone who thinks he’s pure is surely not.” And we know that O’Connor did not think herself pure, for she writes in her prayer journal, “Today I have proved myself a glutton—for Scotch oatmeal cookies and erotic thought. There is nothing left to say of me.” 

Flannery O’Connor sees herself as she sees her characters in her fiction: wounded and in need of healing, weak and in need of strength, human and in need of the Divine, good but always under construction, at least on this side of the veil. That amalgamation of confidence and humility, of agency and dependence, which manifests itself as O’Connor’s authenticity is what I argue has made her, and will continue to make her, a friend and hero of Gen Z.

 

Flannery O’Connor as Interpreter of the Gen Z Experience 

During Lent of 2026 I spent every Wednesday evening with a room packed full of young adults at the cathedral of St. John the Evangelist in downtown Cleveland reading Flannery O’Connor. Over those seven weeks we studied “A Good Man Is Hard to Find,” “The River,” “Good Country People,” “The Enduring Chill,” “Parker’s Back,” “Everything That Rises Must Converge,” and “Revelation.” Although there were some young Millennials present, the majority of those gathered were members of Gen Z, and most had never read Flannery O’Connor. 
What Do Their Deaths Demand
Get This $2 Book!

As you might imagine, the first night was difficult for some, especially those who had heard that O’Connor was a faithful Catholic, only to discover that her most famous story—the one we studied on Ash Wednesday—was about a hard-headed grandmother whose family gets murdered in the woods, and, by the end, she herself takes three rounds to the chest and collapses in a ditch and rests cross-legged in a puddle of her own blood, and that somehow this story is supposed to be about grace. With their foreheads still marked with black crosses of ash, my Gen Z friends looked at me and wanted answers. Slowly, we started to examine characters, identifying qualities of the Grandmother and the Misfit, thinking about which of them would make a better friend and why. We started to ask if there is anything about the Grandmother that reminds us of ourselves. Are we ever self-absorbed? Stubborn? A little racist? Do we ever lie? Have we ever doubted our faith? 

For a Generation that is constantly expected to show only the best experiences of their lives on social media, posting photos and videos that show the good times, the joys, the victories, and the successes, with filters that enhance or even alter reality to some idealistic state, to be able to identify fallen human nature and its need for redemption and healing in the dark comedic literature of Flannery O’Connor can be a welcomed grace. To come to understand that we humans all have parts of ourselves that are not pretty, are not whole, are not healthy, but distorted, deformed, and grotesque—like a missing arm, a missing leg, or a clubfoot—can be a relief, especially when you realize you are not the only one. 

Moreover, it is comforting to know that when Flannery O’Connor was a young adult, she struggled with the same sorts of things that many members of Gen Z are struggling with today. Fear: “I dread, Oh Lord, losing my faith.” Discouragement: “Dear God, I am so discouraged about my work.” Gossip: “I say many many too many uncharitable things about people everyday.” Spiritual desolation: “The summer was very arid spiritually & up here getting to go to Mass again every day has left me unmoved—thoughts awful in their pettiness & selfishness come into my mind even with the host on my tongue.” And the desire to be faithful without abandoning one’s reason: “I would like to be intelligently holy.” 

Just as the COVID-19 pandemic was a significant formative experience for Generation Z, so too was it for Flannery O’Connor, or at least for her legacy. She almost got cancelled. The fact that you are reading this article in this journal is evidence that the violent bear it away and that everything that rises must converge. It is mysteries like these, on full display in the life and art of Flannery O’Connor, that I think will hold Gen Z’s attention for some time.
